1:
The chapter wheels away from the honour of the one before it, and the witnesses hear in Job's abrupt "but now" the hinge on which his whole lament will turn. The reformed John Gill is careful to say whom these mockers are not: not the three friends, who were men in years and not all younger than he, nor men of mean birth, for with such Job would never have kept company in his prosperity, their fathers being in all likelihood both great and good; the derision comes rather from a set of profligate and abandoned wretches who, the moment his troubles fell, jeered him by word and gesture. To be had "in derision" is the common lot of good men, Gill grants, but to be so used by juniors and inferiors is the sharpest aggravation of it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the verse directly against ch. 29:8, where the youth had risen and hidden themselves in reverence; now that Job is no longer affluent they are no longer respectful, and to be reckoned beneath the very "dogs of my flock" — men not fit to be trusted with the curs that guarded the sheep, let alone made shepherds or camel-drivers — is, he says, an expression of sovereign contempt. John Wesley presses the same point of nature: custom and the light of nature alike taught the young to reverence their elders, yet these, whose fathers' condition was so mean that in the world's opinion they were unworthy to be his shepherds and the companions of his dogs, now deride him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry opens here the long complaint that the meanness of the persons who affronted him doubles the disgrace of a once-honoured man. As princes and nobles had deferred to him in prosperity, so now he is spurned by the basest of mankind; and Henry guards one nicety of the sense, that Job "speaks of what he might have done, not of what he did," for he knew the dignity of human nature too well actually to set any of the children of men with the dogs of his flock. Here the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parts company on the grammar, rendering the clause not as a suppressed wish but a plain past fact — "whose fathers I disdained to set" — the sting being that the children of men so far beneath him should now treat him thus. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, hold the whole reversal in a phrase: the man once an object of reverential fear to the respectable youth of the city is now the sport of its vagabonds, the reverence of former days displaced by their laughter. The witnesses divide only over the mood of the verb, whether Job merely might have disdained those fathers or actually did; on the bitterness of the reversal itself they are wholly one.
2:
From the sons the witnesses turn to the fathers, and to the barbed question "whereto might the strength of their hands profit me." The reformed John Gill reads it of men who, lusty and able-bodied as they were, kept their strength only to fold their hands in their bosom; so slothful were they that Job could have put them to no profitable business, which is one reason he would not so much as set them with the dogs of his flock. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line, "the strength of their hands, what should it profit me? — they have lost vigour and strength," and note the artistry of the Hebrew: the disproportionately long opening line, marked off by its accents, is meant to form a deep, long-breathed beginning to the lamentation, the particle rendered "but now" marking the very turning-point from Job's former estate to his present grief. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical witness, fixes the reference of the pronouns — this verse still describes the fathers, while the verses that follow describe their children — and identifies the whole tribe with a people much like the Troglodytes of Herodotus, cave-dwellers who led an outcast life with manners of their own, an alien and proscribed race with whom Job must once have been familiar.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees the fathers are in view and glosses the obscure close, "their old age also has perished": Job never esteemed their strength even in its vigour, nor their counsel in age, so that as their youth was without profit their old age was without honour. Clarke records too the bolder proposal of Mr. Good, that the words are really Arabic and should be joined to the next verse and rendered, "with whom crabbed looks are perpetual, from hunger and flinty famine" — a reading that keeps close to the drift of the received text even while treating its principal words as Arabic. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers both generations into one verdict of uselessness: they and their families were the unprofitable burdens of the earth, and Job with all his prudence could make nothing of them. The young were not fit for labour, so lazy and awkward at their work; the old were not to be advised with in the smallest matter, "for in them was old age indeed, but their old age was perished — they were twice children." The witnesses do not divide over the sense: whether the strength be reckoned worthless in youth or the age dishonoured, these fathers were good for nothing to a man who could make nothing of them, and the mockery of such men is the measure of how far he has fallen.
3:
Driven by "want and famine" into the waste, this outcast race is next described by its very destitution, and the witnesses trace the wording of it. The reformed John Gill notes the Targum's turn, "without children," but prefers to read the difficult word of a people reduced through famine to the utmost extremity, as destitute as a rock or a hard flint from which nothing at all can be got. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line, "they are benumbed from want and hunger, they who gnaw the steppe, the darkness of the wilderness and waste," making the desert itself their gnawed and cheerless pasture. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "fleeing into the wilderness" as the very extreme of want, when the barren desert is supposed the only place where anything to sustain life can be found; while John Wesley catches a different note in the word "solitary": though want commonly drives men toward the haunts of others for relief, these were so conscious of their own guilt that they shunned all company, and for fear or shame fled away to live in desolate places. A real difference of rendering thus stirs beneath the word: whether it means Job's mockers were reduced to a barren solitude like the flint, benumbed with famine, as Gill and Keil have it, or that they deliberately fled the eyes of men, as Wesley reads it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the moral of the picture without softening its misery. They were extremely poor, ready to starve, for they would not dig and to beg they were ashamed; and being brought into their straits not by the providence of God but by their own slothfulness and wastefulness, no neighbour was forward to relieve them. So they were forced to flee into the deserts both for shelter and for sustenance, put to sorry shifts indeed. Henry will own the righteousness of God in it — that slothfulness clothes men with rags and the idle soul is made to suffer hunger — yet he bids the well-fed remember that "one half of the world does not know how the other half lives," and that those who have abundance ought sometimes to think of those whose fare is so coarse. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil weigh the barren steppe and the flinty want, Clarke and Wesley the flight into the wilderness and the guilt that drove it there, and Henry the sloth that ripened into famine; together they set before the reader the wretched stock from which Job's mockers sprang, so that the contempt of such men might be felt as the very bottom of his humiliation.
4:
The witnesses turn botanist over the outcasts' fare — "who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat" — and the identification of the plants becomes a small learned contest. The reformed John Gill rehearses the long dispute over the first: not the common mallow, which is no tree-shrub and is medicine rather than food, but something salt, so that Broughton renders it "salt herbs" and Grotius thinks of the growth by a salt marsh; the Septuagint's word points to the halimus of Dioscorides and Galen, the sea-purslain that the meaner sort ate. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix it as the tall shrubby orach, the sea-purslain whose buds and young leaves the poor gather, and cite the Talmudic tale of King Jannai, who on returning from the desert had these same malluach served on golden tables in memory of the fathers who ate them in their poverty. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke derives the word from the root for "salt" and agrees on the saltwort or sea-purslane, and then labours the harder puzzle of the second plant: the broom or juniper, so named, he thinks, from a root meaning "to bind," whose roots it seems strange to eat at all.

Indeed Clarke half doubts whether the roots were eaten, since the juniper's chief virtue was its fierce and lasting coals — the "coals of juniper" of Ps. 120:4 — and wonders if the clause should rather mean the wood that baked their bread; but he settles the doubt with a witness from the far north, the Gothic archbishop Olaus Magnus, who testifies that among his own people the very roots of the juniper were eaten for bread in time of famine, hard as they were to come at for the prickles. John Wesley keeps to the plainest sense: the "mallows" are bitter herbs that show the outcasts' extreme necessity, and as for the "juniper," the word may signify some other plant, "for the Hebrews themselves are at a loss for the signification of the names of plants." The witnesses do not divide over the misery the verse paints, only over the botany that conveys it — whether salt sea-purslain or bitter herb, whether the broom's root gnawed for bread or its wood burned to bake it. What all agree is that men reduced to grubbing such roots and leaves from the desert scrub are the men who now make Job their jest, and the pathos of the picture is that Job, describing their want so exactly, must once have looked on it with pity.
5:
Cast out of all settled life, the outcasts are next seen "driven forth from among men," and the witnesses weigh both the fact and the cry that pursued it. The reformed John Gill takes the expulsion in its plainest force: they were driven from towns and cities and all civil society as unfit to remain in it, and not for any good but for their crimes, like felons or transported men put away from honest neighbourhoods. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the scene from life — persons whom no one would employ, chased away from the city, and if any of them appeared the hue and cry was raised at once; he notes that the last clause, which the Authorized Version gives as "they cried after them as after a thief," is turned by Mr. Good the other way, "they slunk away from them like a thief," so that it is a question whether the pursuers shout or the outcasts skulk.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry paints them at their fullest length as the scandal and plague of the places they haunted, arrant scoundrels and the scum of the country: so lying, thieving, lurking, and mischievous that the best service the magistrates could do was to rid the land of them, "while the very mob cried after them as after a thief — Away with such fellows from the earth; it is not fit they should live." Yet Henry keeps the justice of the case in view. They were lazy and would not work, and were therefore justly exclaimed against as thieves, "for those that do not earn their own bread by honest labour do, in effect, steal the bread out of other people's mouths"; an idle fellow is a public nuisance, though Henry adds the shrewd note that it were better to drive such into a workhouse than into a wilderness, which will punish them indeed but never reform them. The witnesses do not divide over the wretchedness or the guilt of these men. Gill and Henry mark the crimes that earned their banishment, and both weigh the irony that once bore hard on Job: it was he, in the day of his power, who had put in force the very laws against such vagrants, and it is these same driven men who now, seeing him brought low, cry after him as once the country cried after them. Whether the closing clause be read of their shouting or their slinking, the verse fixes the mockers as men themselves cast out, and their scorn as the revenge of the rejected.
6:
Homeless and hunted, the outcasts are lodged where only beasts will lodge — "to dwell in the cliffs of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks" — and the witnesses attend to the wording of their wretched shelter. The reformed John Gill glosses the first term of the "valleys" or "brooks," the hollow places scooped out by floods and streams of water, into which these men crept for want of any roof. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the whole line to the same effect and set it in its larger frame: the men here described, degraded alike in condition and in character, are the very rabble whose wrongs Job had once pitied in an earlier chapter and who now, when their marauding brings them onto his domain, make sport of the sufferer. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as the plain record of a people obliged to take shelter in the most dangerous, out-of-the-way, and unfrequented places, driven by their outlawry into holes where no settled man would live.

The picture belongs to the movement of Job's lament as much as to its geography. He is not, the witnesses agree, cataloguing a strange tribe for its own sake but heaping up the tokens of its baseness, so that the contempt of such creatures may weigh the heavier. Keil and Delitzsch are the fullest here, and they insist that the men of this strophe are no other than those of the one before — the same wild and pauperized folk, now viewed from the side of their coarse and degenerate manner of life, as they had before been viewed from the side of the wrong done to them. That double view is itself telling: Job, who once looked on their misery with something like compassion, now feels the whole of it turned against him, for the wretches he might have relieved are the wretches who deride him. The witnesses do not divide over the sense. Gill fixes the flood-worn clefts, Clarke the unfrequented and perilous hiding-places, Keil and Delitzsch the moral and social ruin that drove men to such dens; and together they complete the portrait of a people who dwell like the conies among the rocks and the wild things in the caves, so that when Job says he has become their song, the reader may measure how low the song has come from. The lodging of beasts breeds the manners of beasts, and it is those manners that will presently be loosed upon him.
7:
The manners of the den now break into sound, for "among the bushes they brayed," and the witnesses listen to the noise and dispute its very letters. The reformed John Gill hears in it the cry of men likened to wild asses, or else a groaning and moaning among the bushes where they lurked, whether through cold or through hunger, since the wild ass brays not but when it is in want. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees they cried out among the bushes seeking food as the wild ass in its want, but records a textual nicety — that two manuscripts read "they groaned" for "they brayed," a single letter altering the beast's cry to a man's — and takes the "nettles" of the second clause as briers or brambles under which they huddled together like wild beasts. John Wesley keeps the plainer image: they brayed like wild asses for hunger or thirst, and hid themselves under the thorns lest they be discovered when sought out for justice.

The grammatical-historical witnesses add both the antiquity and the tense. Charles Ellicott recalls that Herodotus said the speech of such cave-dwellers was like the screeching of bats, others like the whistling of birds; and he makes a point that governs the reading of the whole passage, that "this whole description is of the mockers of Job, and therefore should be in the present tense" — these are not a people of the distant past but the very men now loosed against him. Keil and Delitzsch tell how miserably such creatures shift for themselves in every season: naked they pass the night, having nothing on the body and no covering in the cold, and are drenched by the mountain storms with no shelter but the bushes under which they crouch; and they add the traveller's note that the wandering folk of the steppe to this day sleep so, many perishing when snow or an enemy overtakes them. Gill fills out the beast-likeness from the natural fact that the wild ass "brays not but when in want," so that the very braying is the cry of hunger, and the men who utter it are known by it for the famished vagrants they are. The witnesses do not finally divide, though a genuine difference of reading runs beneath their agreement — whether the outcasts "bray" like beasts or "groan" like broken men, a difference of one Hebrew letter that Clarke alone weighs. What none of them doubts is the degradation the verse fixes: men who herd under the brambles and cry like asses for their food are the men whose scorn Job must now endure, and Ellicott's insistence on the present tense keeps the whole miserable tribe standing, living and jeering, before the sufferer's eyes.
8:
The pedigree of the mockers is summed in a phrase of contempt — "children of fools, yea, children of base men" — and the witnesses probe both the word and its rendering. The reformed John Gill weighs the sense of "fool": not that these were idiots, wholly void of reason, but men of slender capacity, "Nabal-like," as the name in the Hebrew hints; and he leans rather to the stronger biblical use of the word, so common in the Psalms and Proverbs, where the "fool" is the wicked man — for these could be shrewd enough to do evil, however dull they were to any good. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the first clause as "children of nabal, children without a name," persons of no consideration and the descendants of such; and on the second he departs from the older version, taking "viler than the earth" rather as "driven out of the land," men not fit for civil society. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott joins him precisely here, rendering the close not "viler than the earth" but "they are scourged out of the land," outcasts expelled from among men.

So a real difference of rendering divides the witnesses over the last clause: whether the poet says these men were baser than the very ground they trod, as the Authorized Version and Gill's reading have it, or that they were whipped and driven out of the land, as Clarke and Ellicott prefer. Keil and Delitzsch, giving the verse in translation, keep the older sense, "they were viler than the earth." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who had run through the whole degraded catalogue, ends it on the same note of nameless baseness: they were "a vile kind, yea, a kind without fame," people to whom nobody could give a good word or wish a good wish, banished from the earth as being viler than the earth, so low sunk that "one would not think it possible that ever the human nature should sink so low." Henry draws from it the sober thanksgiving that when we bless God that we are men we have reason to bless him that we are not such men, so far had the human nature sunk and degenerated in this abject and nameless brood. The witnesses do not divide over the degradation the verse pronounces, only over the exact turn of its last words; and all agree that Job's point is bitterest here, that the scorn now heaped on him comes from the most despised of all mankind.
9:
"And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword" — with the second "but now" the lament turns from the mockers to the mockery itself, and the witnesses feel the full sting of it. The reformed John Gill hears Job made the very subject of their song, a man of whom ballads were sung in the public places and at their merriments, even as the Psalmist was "the song of the drunkards"; or else the sense is that they made merry over his calamities, a cruelty like that of the Edomites rejoicing in the day of Judah's destruction. To be the byword of the base, Gill implies, is to be handed round as a proverb of scorn, one's very name become a jest in the mouths of men one would once have disdained. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts it in a sentence: "I am the subject of their mirth, and serve as a proverb or by-word; they use me with every species of indignity."

The grammatical-historical witnesses mark the structure and the deeper resonance. Keil and Delitzsch note that this is the second of the three great "but now" clauses that shape the elegy, each beginning a fresh movement of the complaint, so that here the sufferer's disgrace is taken up anew and driven home. Charles Ellicott points to the margin and its cross-references, which show, he says, that it is "quite appropriate to give to the complaints of Job a Messianic interpretation" — for the innocent man made the drunkard's song and the people's byword foreshadows a greater sufferer still. Gill had touched the same chord, setting Job's usage beside that of Christ, the antitype who was likewise the song of the scornful. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the bitterness of the verse lies not in any bodily pang but in the ruin of a good name, that the honour of ch. 29, where every ear that heard him blessed him, has been exactly reversed, so that the tongues which once praised now taunt. And they agree that a spirit so ingenuous as Job's feels this reversal as one of the sharpest of his afflictions: to have become a jest is, to such a man, a wound as deep as the sores upon his skin, and the reader is meant to hear, under the taunting song, the movement of a grief that has passed from the loss of goods and health to the loss of all esteem.
10:
The scorn now takes on a bodily insolence — "they spare not to spit in my face" — and the witnesses read both the loathing and the meaning of the spittle. The reformed John Gill finds it no wonder that such men abhorred him when his own intimate friends had drawn back; and he insists that they abhorred him not for any evil in him but for the good — for the reproof his very integrity carried to them — and for his present meanness, poverty, and disease, so that here again he sees a type of Christ, whom the rulers of his own people abhorred and set at nought, preferring a robber and murderer to him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the verse in its stark order — they abhor him, flee far from him, and withhold not their spittle from his face — reading it of the same degraded rabble whose contempt has now grown openly abusive. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts his eyes from Job to the age that allowed it: "what a state must civil society be in, when such indignities were permitted to be offered to the aged and afflicted!"

On the spitting itself the witnesses part a little. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, will not take it to the letter, since the mockers "kept far from him" and could not literally reach his face; he reads it figuratively of every kind of reproachful expression flung at him, "even to my face," and hears in it once more the type of Christ, made a reproach of men and despised of the people. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch let the word stand nearer its plain force, an actual gesture of loathing, however the fleeing crowd might contrive it, the spittle the last and lowest token of a contempt that no longer even fears him. So a genuine difference runs beneath the verse — whether the "spitting" be real spittle or the spat-out words of scorn — yet it is a difference only of the figure, not of the fact, for all agree that Job is treated as a thing unclean, shunned and reviled at once. The movement of the lament is plain in it: the man who a moment ago was merely their song is now the object of a physical revulsion, fled from as a leper and insulted as an outcast, and the witnesses hear in the very extremity of it the foreshadowing of another face that men hid from and did not spare.
11:
Job traces the whole insolence back to a single loosed cord — "because he hath loosed my cord, and afflicted me" — and over that cord the witnesses fall into their sharpest dispute of the chapter. The reformed John Gill spreads out its possible senses: not the silver cord of life, for then he had died at once, but perhaps the loosened nerves of a body broken by disease, or the untwisted state of a family and substance once bound firmly together, or best of all the cord of his magistracy, the authority with which he had bound many to reverence and obedience, now slackened so that the baser sort dare insult him. Gill then lays bare the textual fact that governs the reading, that the marginal Hebrew has "my cord" — which the Authorized Version follows — while the written text has "his cord," which Broughton renders "he hath loosed his string," the rein of government by which the mighty hold base men in check.

That written reading opens the door to the archer's image the other witnesses prefer. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes "his cord" as the bowstring of God, who like an archer has set his arrow on the string, drawn it to the full, and loosed it against Job — a figure the Vulgate and Septuagint support with their "he hath opened his quiver"; and the second clause he reads of men who, seeing God afflict him, threw off all restraint like headstrong horses that have got the bit in their teeth. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, judges the written text plainly better: "God hath loosed the cord of his bow, and they have cast off all restraint before me." John Wesley reads it the same way — God has slackened the string of his bow and so rendered his defence useless, and the mockers, freed of every former restraint of humanity and modesty, now do to his face what once they trembled lest he should so much as hear. So the debate is real and turns on a single letter: whether Job's own cord — his life, his authority, his estate — has been loosed, as Gill's reading allows, or God's bowstring has been let slip to shoot him down and to loose the rabble upon him, as Clarke, Ellicott, and Wesley prefer. The witnesses agree only on the double sense of the second clause, that the loosing of Job's restraints was at once the loosing of theirs: the hand of God withdrawn from him became the signal for every base tongue to be let go.
12:
The assault grows organized, and Job feels it press on the very side where his accusers would stand — "upon my right hand rise the youth" — a phrase the witnesses read at once of a courtroom and of a siege. The reformed John Gill dwells on the odd word for these youths, one that suggests young birds scarce out of the shell, unfledged striplings just sprung into being, who rose up not in the old reverence but in open hostility, taking the right hand of him as though they were his betters. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees the term means buds or "younglings," and renders the middle clause vividly: they "push away my feet," trip up his heels and trample him, then "roll themselves upon me" as one wave drives on another, washing the sand from under a man's feet till he sinks. John Wesley supplies the double figure that holds the verse together: the right hand is "the place of adversaries or accusers in courts of justice," where these young striplings, who once hid themselves from his presence, now stand to arraign him; and their "ways of destruction" are like the banks that soldiers cast up against a besieged city, thrown against him to bring him down.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps the rendering lean — "the youth" are simply the young brood, the rabble — but the picture the witnesses build together is anything but lean. Job is at once a defendant with the mob crowding the accuser's side of the court and a walled city with the enemy raising his siege-works against it, and both images serve the one grief, that the meanest of men have taken the posture of his judges and besiegers. Keil and Delitzsch, giving the strophe in translation, join this verse to the two that follow as one sustained assault, the rabble pressing on his right, thrusting his feet from under him, and casting up their destructive ways. Gill notes that some would even read the word as "the flower," the chief and choicest of men, but he rejects it, keeping to the beardless striplings whose insolence is the sharper for their youth. The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only over the shading of the single word for the youth — whether unfledged nestlings, buds, or brood — and all agree that the horror of the verse is its inversion of ch. 29:8: the young who once withdrew in awe now rise up in arms, and the man who once sat as a prince in the gate is beset as a prisoner and stormed as a stronghold.
13:
The siege presses closer as the assailants "mar my path," and the witnesses divide over what path is meant and how it is marred. The reformed John Gill reads it inwardly, of men who hindered Job in the exercise of religion, who would not suffer him to walk in the ways of holiness, or who reproached and triumphed over his holy conversation. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the figure of the besieged city he had begun: they "destroy the way-marks," tear up the guide-posts so that there is no safe travelling, even as besiegers stop the fountains and break the roads and raise their engines against the walls; and he takes the closing "they have no helper" from Mr. Good as "there is not an adviser among them," none to give them any better counsel. John Wesley reads the marred path as the stopping of all Job's ways out of his misery, and "set forward my calamity" of men who increase his affliction by their invectives and censures — "even they," he marvels, "who are themselves in a forlorn and miserable condition."

The grammatical-historical witnesses sharpen both the verb and the last clause. Keil and Delitzsch render the opening "they tear down my path," insisting the word means to pull down, as one demolishes a road, not to tear open, and read the whole of men who "minister to my overthrow, they who themselves are helpless." Charles Ellicott glosses the same closing phrase differently, taking "they have no helper" to mean that they wreak all this mischief "probably without deriving therefrom any help or advantage themselves" — malice with nothing to gain, and needing none, for they are fools in all else yet wise enough to do hurt. So the witnesses part on more than one point: whether the marred path is Job's course of godliness or the literal road broken up in a siege, and whether the men "have no helper" because they are themselves too wretched to have one, as Wesley and Keil hold, or because their cruelty profits them nothing, as Ellicott judges. Yet beneath the differences the movement of the lament is single and clear. Job pictures himself hemmed in on every side, his ways of escape pulled down before him, his ruin hurried forward by hands that gain nothing by it; and the very helplessness of his tormentors — driven, degraded men adding to the grief of a greater sufferer — is itself part of the bitterness, that so much malice should come from so much misery.
14:
The pent-up assault at last bursts through, and Job likens it to a flood loosed through a shattered wall — "they came upon me as a wide breaking in of waters." The reformed John Gill draws out the double image the words carry: as when a broad breach is made in the banks of a river or the sea and the waters rush through in irresistible abundance, or as when a wide gap is torn in the wall of a besieged city and the soldiers pour in and bear down all before them, so Job's enemies rushed upon him in their numbers and overwhelmed him at a stroke. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the figure of the siege carried on from the verses before, and tie the "breach" back to Job's earlier cry that God had broken him "with breach upon breach" in ch. 16:14: he is become as a wall with a wide-gaping rent, through which the rabble storm in to make him wholly their prey.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same picture in its sequence — the sap, the breach, the storm, the flight, the pursuit — and sees the assailants, once the breach is made, roll in upon him as an irresistible torrent. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the difficult second word, offering "as through a wide breach they come; in the midst of the crash they roll themselves upon me," or, taking the term otherwise, "instead of a tempest they roll themselves upon me." So a genuine question of rendering runs through the verse, over the word the Authorized Version gives as "in the desolation": whether it names the desolation into which they roll, the crash of the falling wall under which they surge, or the tempest they come on like. Yet the witnesses do not divide over the force of the whole. Whether flood or storm or stormed city, the image is of an overwhelming and pitiless rush, a mass of men pouring in through a ruin already made — for the wall was broken, Keil reminds us, by the decrees of God before ever the rabble came — and rolling themselves upon the sufferer as waves roll, taking a savage pleasure in the desolation. Gill marks how the assailants take a savage delight in it, rolling themselves upon him as a man rolls in an easy bed, wallowing in the ruin they have made. The lament has reached the height of its picture of human cruelty; the next verse will turn from the besiegers to the terror they leave in the soul.
15:
With the third "but now" the elegy begins afresh, and the witnesses hear the complaint turn inward from the mockers to the terror they have bred — "terrors are turned upon me." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark this as the last of the three great turning-points that shape the poem, each opening a new movement of the lament; and they render the verse of terrors that pursue "my nobility like the wind, and like a cloud my prosperity passed away." The reformed John Gill is careful to say what these terrors are not: not the terrors of a guilty conscience, for Job held fast his integrity; not the terrors of a condemning law, for he knew his living Redeemer; not the terrors of death, which he had made familiar and even desired; nor of the judgment, before which he longed to be tried; but the terrors of God's afflicting hand now turned against him, his face hidden, his favour withheld, so that the sufferer is thrown into a consternation of mind.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry opens here his account of what he calls the sorest part of the whole calamity, the trouble that seized the soul. If Job looked forward, everything was frightful before him; if he strove to shake the terrors off, they turned furiously upon him; if he sought to flee, they pursued his soul as swiftly and violently as the wind, even as he had complained at the first of the terrors of God setting themselves in array against him in ch. 6:4. Henry lingers over the word the Authorized Version gives as "my soul," noting that the Hebrew is "my principal one, my princess," the soul being the noblest part of the man, our very glory, so that what pursues the soul is most of all to be dreaded. And if Job looked back, he saw his welfare and prosperity pass away "as suddenly, swiftly, and irrecoverably as a cloud." Here the witnesses differ only in the shade of a word: where Henry reads the fleeing thing as Job's princely soul, Keil and Delitzsch read it as his "nobility," the dignity and estate that the terrors chase away like wind-driven cloud. On the substance they are wholly one. The lament has passed from the outward assault of men to the inward pursuit of dread; the terrors that stormed the walls are now within, hunting the soul itself, and the good that once was Job's is gone like vapour, leaving him to the days of affliction that the next verse will name.
16:
The pursuing terrors leave the soul spent and running out like water, and Job says so in a figure the witnesses handle with care — "and now my soul is poured out upon me." The reformed John Gill offers its senses in a rising order: the soul poured out in prayer, or dissolved in a flood of tears at his distress, or, deeper still, the very spirits sunk and the heart melted, the soul pouring itself out unto death as a vessel full of holes lets its liquor run away, so that his life seemed to be ebbing from him and his vital powers almost spent. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "and now my soul is poured out within me, days of suffering hold me fast," and explain the image of a soul poured out within a man as one that, yielding itself without resistance to sadness, sinks to its very bottom, its whole frame as it were flowing together in grief.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both clauses as the seizure and the sinking of a broken man. The "days of affliction" have "taken hold upon me," he reads, have arrested him as a bailiff claps his hand on a debtor's back and secures him; for when trouble comes with commission it takes fast hold and will not let go. And Henry hears in the poured-out soul the last inward failure, the spirit "not only wounded but poured out upon him," Job "not only weak as water, but, in his own apprehension, lost as water spilt upon the ground," like the Psalmist whose heart was "melted like wax" in Ps. 22:14. Henry notes too that Job reckons his misery by days, which will soon be numbered and finished, and are nothing to the ages of eternity, a comfort he draws from 2 Cor. 4:17; the affliction that seizes so fast is yet an affliction bounded by days, and days that heaven has counted. The witnesses do not divide. Gill traces the soul running out toward death, Keil the soul sinking under sadness to its depths, Henry the days of grief that seize and hold; and all three read the verse as the low point of the inward complaint, where the man who had withstood the loss of goods and children and health feels at last his very soul dissolving within him — and yet, as the reckoning by days quietly hints, dissolving toward an end that God has numbered and will not let outrun its term.
17:
From the failing soul the lament sinks into the aching frame, and to the long nights when "my bones are pierced in me in the night season." The reformed John Gill reads it of a disease that penetrated to the very bones and their marrow, with such pain in the muscles and joints as if all his bones were piercing and breaking to pieces — and this in the night, the hour meant for rest, when the sufferer should have been refreshed with sleep and instead found only torment; some, he notes, would even make the night itself the piercer, as Broughton renders it, "the night pierced my bones from me." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep that bolder rendering, "the night rendeth my bones from me, and my gnawers sleep not," taking the second clause not of resting sinews but of gnawing pains that never lie still — the very griefs personified as creatures that will not sleep while their victim aches.

So the witnesses part over the wording of the second line: whether it be Job's "sinews" that take no rest, as the Authorized Version and Gill's reading have it, or his "gnawers," the boring pains that never slumber, as Keil and Delitzsch prefer; and whether the piercing be done by the disease within or by the night itself, that long dark stretch which seems to saw his bones from his body. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, weighing the same misery, calls it a sword in his bones that pierced him in the night, his nerves affected with strong convulsions, his sinews taking no rest, so that "by reason of his pain he could take no rest, but sleep departed from his eyes." Gill adds that the sufferer here is like those broken men of the Psalms who found no soundness in their bones and no rest in the night watches, the disease boring inward where it could least be borne. The witnesses do not divide over the anguish, only over the figure that conveys it. What all set before us is the peculiar cruelty of a pain that comes in the night, when the whole world is still and the sufferer alone is awake to feel his bones bored through, his very rest turned into a fresh scene of torment. The movement of the lament is plain: it has descended from the terror of the soul to the ache of the skeleton, and the night, which for other men closes the day's grief, only opens Job's afresh, his gnawing pains keeping watch while all else sleeps.
18:
The disease has so worked upon him that even his clothing is altered, and the witnesses divide over what exactly is changed — "by the great force of my disease is my garment changed." The reformed John Gill offers the plainer possibilities: the colour of the garment changed by the purulent matter running from his sores, or the frequent shifting of raiment his condition forced, or, dropping the added words "of my disease," the garment changed with great force and difficulty because it clung so close to his ulcerated body. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the "garment" rather of the skin itself, the whole body wrapped in a kind of elephantine hide formed by the incrustations of the disease, a new covering as closely attached to him as the collar of his coat; though he offers a second image too, of the malady seizing him "as a strong armed man," throttling him and casting him into the mud like a wrestler who has thrown his opponent.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the crux hardest. Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the word means the skin — "the covering of my body is distorted," crust forming after crust — but decide for the strict sense, "by divine omnipotence my garment is distorted, becomes unlike itself, and like the collar of my shirt it fits close to me," taking "the great force" to be the force of God rather than of the sickness. Charles Ellicott catalogues both, "by His great power the garment of my skin is disfigured," or "with great effort must my garment be changed because of the sores to which it clings; it bindeth me about as closely as the collar of my coat." So a genuine double debate runs through the verse: whether the thing "changed" is the literal garment or the diseased skin worn like a garment, and whether "the great force" is the violence of the malady or the omnipotence of God who sends it. Clarke presses his wrestler's image a step further, of the disease seizing him by the throat, bringing him down, and treading him in the dirt, as the stronger of two grapplers throws and pins the weaker; while Gill keeps the homelier picture of a garment whose very colour is changed by the matter that runs from the sores. The witnesses do not divide over the wretchedness the verse conveys — a man so corrupted that his very covering is disfigured and binds him like a throttling collar — but they leave the reader to choose between the ruined cloak and the ruined skin, and between the disease and the divine hand behind it, as the changer of Job's garment.
19:
Now the sufferer names the hand behind it all, and says he has been flung down into filth — "he hath cast me into the mire." The reformed John Gill is careful over the mire: not the mire of sin, into which God casts no man, but the mire of affliction and calamity, in which Job is made as abject and contemptible as if he had been thrown into a kennel and rolled in it; and he ascribes the act to God, done, as Job apprehended it, with something like contempt and indignation. Gill records an old Jewish turn of the words, "it taught me in the mire," as though his ulcers had schooled him to sit down among the ashes; a reading that might yield a good lesson, he allows, since the saints are taught much in affliction, but one he thinks foreign to Job's meaning here.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the movement of the verse within the lament: here Job "now turns more directly to God," having in the verse of his poured-out soul turned from man to his own condition, and closing with the confession that he is become "like dust and ashes." Ellicott notes the rareness of that phrase, used but three times in all Scripture — twice by Job, here and in his final repentance at ch. 42:6, and once by Abraham when he pleaded with God as "dust and ashes" in Gen. 18:27. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse in the same sense, God the caster-down and Job in appearance as dust and ashes. So the witnesses part only over the old Jewish reading Gill weighs and sets aside — whether God "cast" him into the mire or the disease "taught" him to sit in it — and on the main sense they are wholly one. The lament has reached the point to which it was tending all along: Job turns from the rabble that mock him to the God who, as he feels it, has thrown him down into the dirt of his ruin. Gill lets the indignity stand at its full weight, a man made so abject that it is as though he had been flung into a kennel and rolled in its filth, cast down by a hand he still owns to be God's. Yet Ellicott's cross-reference quietly softens the despair, for the very words "dust and ashes" are the words of Abraham's humble pleading and of Job's own final peace, so that the phrase which here sounds like defeat is the same in which he will one day repent and be restored.
20:
Turning full toward God, Job lays his bitterest charge against the silence of heaven — "I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me." The reformed John Gill feels the sharpness of it: that Job should cry for help and God turn a deaf ear, or, hearing, should not answer immediately nor in the way desired, is itself a heavy aggravation of his grief; and he notes that crying is the language of prayer, supposing distress and a vehemence of spirit that will not be quieted. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the whole desolation into the verse — "persecuted by man, afflicted with sore disease, and apparently forsaken of God" — and reads the second clause of a God who sees and yet does nothing: "thou seest my desolate, afflicted state, but thine eye doth not affect thy heart; thou leavest me unsupported to struggle with my adversities."

Beneath that clause a real difference of construction divides the witnesses. The Authorized Version, which Gill follows, supplies into the second half the negative of the first — "I stand up, and thou regardest me not" — as Charles Ellicott observes is done elsewhere, citing the parallel of Ps. 9:18. But Ellicott records the other reading, that Job "stands up in the attitude of prayer, and thou lookest at me" — doing no more, with mute indifference; and Keil and Delitzsch prefer just this sterner sense, "I stand there, and thou lookest fixedly at me," God not failing to regard him but regarding him with a cold, unmoved gaze. John Wesley takes the standing simply of persevering prayer, "I pray importunately and continually," a man who rises to his feet and will not leave off crying though no answer comes. Gill presses the same point, that crying is the very language of prayer, and supposes both a real distress and a vehemence of spirit that cannot be stilled; it is no cold petition but the loud, repeated cry of a man in his extremity. So the witnesses part over whether God does not regard Job at all or regards him and will not stir — whether the horror is a heaven that ignores or a heaven that watches without pity. Yet on the movement of the lament they agree: Job has ceased to answer his human accusers and now presses his suit directly upon God, and the anguish of this stretch of the complaint is not the malice of men but the unanswering silence of the One he most needs to hear him, a silence the harder to bear because he cannot doubt that God sees.
21:
"Thou art become cruel to me" — the boldest word yet, and the witnesses handle it with a mixture of frankness and reserve. The reformed John Gill will not disguise that this is "one of the unbecoming expressions which dropped from Job's lips concerning God." He explains its ground charitably: God had been kind and gracious to Job in providence and in special love, and now, his dispensations wholly altered, it seemed to the sufferer as though the divine affections themselves were changed and his love turned to hatred. But Gill answers the complaint even as he reports it — the love of God to his people is never changed, remaining the same in every state; some of his dealings may wear the appearance of severity, and the instruments he uses may indeed be cruel, yet his heart still yearns over his own, and in the end delivers them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse of a God who "changes himself to a cruel being" toward Job and "with the strength of thy hand makest war upon me," reading it as the height of the sufferer's sense that the very hand once laid on him in blessing is now turned in enmity. The wesleyan-arminian voices soften the charge into appearance. Adam Clarke paraphrases, "thou appearest to treat me with cruelty; I cry for mercy, I trust in thy goodness, and am still left under my afflictions; instead of helping, thou opposest me, and appearest as my enemy." John Wesley reads it as if God "hadst changed thy very nature, which is kind, and merciful, and gracious" — the word marking not what God is but what, to Job's darkened sense, he has seemed to become. The witnesses do not divide over the fact of the complaint, only over how far to let it stand. Gill and Wesley mark it plainly as a hard and mistaken thought, an "unbecoming expression" wrung from a man in the dark; Clarke keeps it to the level of seeming; Keil and Delitzsch let it sound in its full boldness as the cry of one who feels the Almighty's strong hand set against him. And all agree that this is the deepest turn of the lament, where the sufferer, having exhausted his grief against men, arraigns the very God he still calls upon — an arraignment the witnesses take not as unbelief but as the anguish of a faith that cannot let God go even while it accuses him.
22:
The charge of cruelty is pressed into a fierce image of a man snatched up and whirled away — "thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride upon it." The reformed John Gill reads it of Job lifted upon the wind of affliction and tossed about like chaff or stubble or a dry leaf, no more able to withstand it than such things can resist a gale; though he allows the other sense too, that God had first raised him high in prosperity only to cast him the lower, so that the very exaltation was part of the cruelty. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the present ruin: God has so stripped him of all his substance that he is like chaff caught up by the wind, a straw that is the sport of every breeze, and at last dissipated into nothing by the continual agitation. John Wesley reads the same, a man exposed to every storm and calamity, "like chaff or stubble lifted up to the wind and violently tossed hither and thither," his very substance and body well-nigh consumed and his heart melted within him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets out the choice that divides the readings. Some, he says, render it wholly of the present affliction — "thou liftest me up to the wind, and causest me to ride upon it; thou dissolvest me in thy blast" — while others hear in it the contrast between Job's former estate and his present, "thou usedst to raise me and make me ride upon the wind, and now thou dissolvest my substance," comparing the Psalmist's "thou hast lifted me up and cast me down" in Ps. 102:10. So a genuine difference runs through the verse: whether the lifting is itself an act of terror, God catching Job up like chaff to hurl him on the storm, or whether it recalls the height from which he has fallen, the man once borne up in honour now blown away and dissolved. The witnesses do not divide over the end of the figure, the dissolving of his substance into nothing before the power of God, which Gill and Henry alike call the soon-melting of man's estate at the divine breath. What the verse fixes, on either reading, is Job's sense of utter weightlessness in the hand that holds him — a creature no more able to stand before Omnipotence than a leaf before the wind, ridden on the storm and scattered at its will.
23:
From the whirling storm the lament settles into a grim certainty, that all this is driving him toward death — "for I know that thou wilt bring me to death." The reformed John Gill takes it of Job's persuasion that God's present providence would not leave off till it had brought him to the grave, to the very dust from which he was taken; though he grants that, in another sense, every man knows this end without special revelation, death being made necessary by sin and fixed by the decree of God upon all, as all experience confirms save for the two who were translated. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley dwells on the tender name the verse gives the grave, "the house appointed for all living": a narrow, dark, cold house, yet one where we shall rest and be safe, our home and our mother's lap, the common receptacle appointed by him who has set the bounds of all our habitations, for rich and poor alike, "and that shortly."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same phrase as the rendezvous of the race, the place of general assembly where all who have lived must meet; and here he breaks into one of his characteristic flights, quoting at length Blair's poem "The Grave," which personifies death as an insatiable "great man-eater whose every day is carnival," the veriest glutton who, having devoured countless swarms, still gapes for more. The witnesses do not divide over the sense of the verse, only over its temper. Gill hears in it Job's dark conviction that this affliction is his death-sickness; Wesley turns it toward comfort, the grave a resting-place and a home; Clarke lets the terror of the universal devourer sound in borrowed verse. Wesley dwells on the homely comfort of the grave as the place where a man is "gathered to his fathers," the common lot appointed by him who has fixed the bounds of every habitation, so that the darkest house is still one God has made ready. Yet all agree on the movement of the lament here, that Job, having felt himself caught up and dissolved on the wind, now looks steadily to the end of it, and names death not with the desperate longing of his earlier speeches but with a settled certainty. The storm is bearing him to one appointed house, and he knows it; and if his tone is dark, there is under it, as Wesley hears, the ancient hope that even that dark house is one his Redeemer has appointed and where his people rest, so that the road to death is not, in the end, the road out of God's keeping.
24:
Certain of the grave, Job utters one of the darkest and most disputed lines of the chapter, over which the witnesses frankly confess the text obscure — "howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave." The reformed John Gill reads it of God's not stretching out his hand to keep Job back from the grave, nor to fetch him out of it once he is in; for God is able to do either, as he raised the Shunammite's son and the widow's son and Lazarus, but does not usually so interpose, so that Job looks for no such reprieve. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse another way altogether, of the natural instinct of the perishing: "doth not one, however, stretch out the hand in falling? doth he not raise a cry for help on that account in his ruin?" — the drowning man's reach and cry, which Job pleads should be allowed even to him.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses hear in it instead a word of comfort. Adam Clarke paraphrases, "though I suffer here, I shall not suffer hereafter; his displeasure shall not proceed beyond the grave," and takes the hard closing clause with Mr. Good as "surely there, in its ruin, is freedom" — in the sepulchre a freedom from calamity and a rest for the weary. John Wesley reads the same consolation: "the hand of God's wrath will not follow me beyond death; I shall then be safe and easy," and though most men "cry in his destruction," affrighted while the body sinks, Job has nothing to fear therein, "since I know that my redeemer liveth." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, throws up his hands: the verse is "very obscure" and finally "hopelessly uncertain," offering rendering upon rendering — that God will not put forth his hand against a ruinous heap, or will not bring a man to death while he earnestly prays for release — and leaving each reader to make the best sense he can. So the debate here is as real as any in the book, and threefold: whether Job means that God will not reach into the grave to save or to keep him there, or that even a falling man may stretch out his hand and cry, or that beyond the grave God's wrath cannot reach and death is freedom. The witnesses do not pretend to resolve it; they leave the verse standing as one of those places where the darkness of the Hebrew matches the darkness of the grief it utters.
25:
"Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the poor?" — Job pleads his own past compassion as the ground on which he might now look for pity. The reformed John Gill reads it of a man of tender and sympathizing heart, who wept with them that wept and whose bowels yearned over the afflicted, whether their trouble were outward or inward; a temper, he says, that is Godlike, for God is afflicted in all the afflictions of his people, and Christlike, since the living Redeemer is touched with the feeling of his people's infirmities. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the connection that makes the plea: the fellow-feeling Job once showed at the misfortune of others will surely be permitted to him in his own, the seeking of compassion from the compassionate; and they gloss the Hebrew of "him that was in trouble" as the man whose lot in life is hard, and the rare verb of the second line as a genuine grieving, a sadness of soul over the needy.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the verse much the same, though Adam Clarke records a bolder rendering from Mr. Good, "should I not then weep for the ruthless day?" — a lament that his sufferings must last as long as his life; yet Clarke himself keeps the older sense, that Job did mourn for those who suffered in calamity and relieved the distressed according to his power. John Wesley hears in it Job's appeal to his own conscience against the harshness of his friends: "have I now judgment without mercy, because I afforded no mercy to others in misery? No; my conscience acquits me; I did mourn over others in their miseries." Charles Ellicott sets it plainly: Job declares that he has not withheld "that sympathy with sorrow and suffering for which he himself has asked in vain." So the witnesses part only over Good's rendering of the first line — whether Job weeps for the sufferer or for the ruthless day of his own suffering — and otherwise stand together. And they hear in the verse a poignant turn of the lament: the man who cried in vain to an unanswering heaven, and was fled from by pitiless men, now recalls that he himself once wept for the wretched, so that his complaint is not the self-pity of a hard man but the bewilderment of a merciful one, asking why the compassion he freely gave is nowhere returned to him.
26:
The plea of past mercy sharpens into the ache of disappointed hope — "when I looked for good, then evil came unto me." The reformed John Gill draws out the reasonableness of the expectation: having shown such sympathy and pity, Job might well have looked for good, and in his prosperity had looked for its long continuance; even in adversity he did not at first think the trouble would abide, but expected, as good men have reason to expect, that God who is good and does good, who has laid up goodness for them that fear him, would turn again and give him good — and in this he was bitterly disappointed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse in its stark antithesis, "when I looked for good, then evil came; I waited for light, and darkness came," letting the balanced clauses carry the whole weight of the reversal.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks a real development in Job's temper here, setting the verse against his words near the beginning of the book. There, in ch. 3:25, Job had spoken as one who would not be the fool of prosperity, who looked at things on their darker side and dreaded the very evil that came; now he speaks as one who "hoped for the best, and yet, notwithstanding that hope, was disappointed and deceived." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps it short and personal — "yet trouble came upon myself, when I expected it not." Gill grounds Job's hope in the covenant kindness of God, who is good and does good and has laid up goodness for them that fear him, so that godliness has the promise of the life that now is as well as of that which is to come; and it is precisely because the hope was so well grounded that its defeat cut so deep. The witnesses do not divide. Gill weighs the good he had grounds to hope for, Keil the sharp antithesis of the Hebrew, Ellicott the change from a man who braced for the worst to a man betrayed in his hope, Wesley the plain surprise of it. And together they mark a quieter, sadder stretch of the lament, where the loud complaint against men and against God gives way to the simple grief of expectation mocked: Job had waited for light, as any sufferer waits for the turning of the night, and the night only deepened. It is the disappointment, not the pain, that speaks here — the peculiar bitterness of looking for good with real hope and finding evil in its place, of waiting for the dawn and meeting a thicker dark.
27:
The disappointed hope leaves an inward tumult that will not subside — "my bowels boiled, and rested not." The reformed John Gill reads the boiling of the inward parts either literally, of a violent fever burning within him, or figuratively, of the ceaseless agitation of a man under great distress, whose very inwards seethe and find no rest. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it the strong commotion of the bowels that every humane person feels at the sight of one in misery — a turn that ties the verse back to Job's own compassion for the wretched, so that the heart which once boiled with pity now boils with pain. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render it in the present, "my bowels boil, and rest not; days of affliction have overtaken me unawares," keeping the anguish immediate and unhealed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both clauses of the verse as the picture of a grief without intermission. Job's "bowels boiled, and rested not," the sense of his calamity continually preying on his spirits with no pause; and the days of affliction, he says, "prevented me" — that is, came upon him unawares, without giving any previous warning, so that he had made no provision for so evil a day. John Wesley reads the same, that affliction "came upon me suddenly and unexpectedly, when I promised myself peace and prosperity." Gill weighs the two constructions of the boiling side by side — the literal fever that burned in the inward parts, and the figurative seething of a mind under great distress — and lets both stand, since the one aptly images the other. The witnesses do not divide. Whether the boiling within be a literal fever or the churning of an anguished mind, and whether the days "prevented" him by anticipating his hope or by surprising his security, all agree on the note the verse sounds: a suffering that neither rests by day nor was looked for before it came, the affliction preying on the spirits without truce or warning. The lament has grown quieter than in its stormy middle, but not calmer; the tumult has moved inward, to the seething of the very bowels, and the man who a verse ago waited for light now feels only the unresting heat of his trouble and the memory of how unforeseen it fell. It is the restlessness of grief, the affliction that gives no truce, that Henry and Wesley alike hear in the boiling that will not settle.
28:
The inward heat shows itself in a darkened face and a broken cry, and the witnesses divide at once over the wording — "I went mourning without the sun." The reformed John Gill offers two constructions: either that Job, overwhelmed with grief, refused all the comfort of the sunshine and went, as Broughton has it, "out of the sun," in mourning black; or that the words mean "I go black, but not by the sun," his face and skin darkened not by the sun's scorching but by the force of his disease, so that he looked like a dweller in the tents of Kedar. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the dispute further still, for the Hebrew word may be drawn from a root meaning to hide or protect, giving "I went mourning without a protector," or from a root meaning to be hot, giving the Vulgate's "without fury" — Calmet's "I walked in deep sadness, but did not give way to an angry spirit."

The grammatical-historical witnesses weigh the same choices and lean to the sun. Charles Ellicott renders "I go mourning without the sun," though he records the alternative "blackened, but not by the sun," and gives his preference to the former; and on the next clause, "I stood up, and I cried in the congregation," he notes that Job cried "not merely in secret, but in the face of all men." Keil and Delitzsch take the mourning garb strictly, the word denoting the dirty-black dress of mourners rather than any leprous discoloration of the skin, and render "I wandered about in mourning without the sun; I rose in the assembly, I gave free course to my complaint." So the debate over the single phrase is genuine and threefold: whether Job went deprived of the sun's light and comfort, or blackened in face but not by the sun, or without a guardian, or without anger. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the public shame of the second clause, that when Job came into the congregation he could not stand up calmly to join the worship, but "stood up and cried aloud," through pain of body or anguish of mind, like one half distracted. The witnesses do not divide over the misery — a man gone black with grief and crying out where all could hear — but they leave the exact colour of "without the sun" for each reader to settle, so tangled is the little word that carries it.
29:
"I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls" — Job likens himself to the mournful creatures of the waste, and the witnesses dispute both the beasts and the brotherhood. The reformed John Gill notes that the ancient versions read "ostriches" for the second, and gathers the several senses of the kinship: that Job was forced to dwell among men as venomous as such creatures, or that he was like them in his solitude, all his friends standing far off while these things love the desolate places, or, likeliest, that his mournful notes resembled their wailing and howling cry, which none regards or pities. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the resemblance in the cry: "by my mournful and continual cry I resemble" the jackals or hyenas, and the "daughters of howling," the ostriches — both, on Dodd's authority, remarkable for their mournful voice and their haunting of desolate places. John Wesley reads it the same, "a brother by imitation of their cries," since persons of like qualities are called brethren, the dragon being the beast "which howl and wail mournfully in the deserts."

The grammatical-historical witnesses confirm the renderings and the note. Charles Ellicott observes that the "dragons and owls" are, according to some moderns, "jackals and ostriches"; Keil and Delitzsch render "I am become a brother of the jackals and a companion of ostriches," and mark that here for the first time Job speaks directly of his disfigurement by leprosy. So a real question of translation runs through the verse — whether the creatures be dragons and owls, as the older versions and Gill have them, or jackals and ostriches, as the moderns prefer — but the point of the likeness stands unshaken on either reading. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds together the two strands the others separate: Job is a brother to these creatures both in choosing solitude and retirement, as they do in the waste places of Isa. 34:13, and in making a fearful, hideous noise, his inconsiderate complaints being fitly compared to their inarticulate cries. Gill draws the last strand of pathos from the cry itself: as these creatures howl and wail in the waste and no man pities or regards them, so Job might cry in the most public place and find none to have compassion on him, his grief as unheeded as the night-cry of a jackal. The witnesses do not divide over the sense: whether by his loneliness or by his howling grief, Job has been driven out of human fellowship into the company of the wild and the mournful, and the man who once sat chief among the living now owns the beasts of the desert for his only kin.
30:
The likeness to the desert creatures is grounded in the ruin of his very body — "my skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat." The reformed John Gill reads the blackened skin either of a deep melancholy, such as darkens the countenance of the sorrowful, or, more likely, of the force of the disease itself, the burning ulcers and black scabs that covered him as famine had blackened the captives of old. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the black skin rather of continual exposure to the open air and the parching sun, and reads the second clause as "a strong expression to point out the raging fever that was continually preying upon his vitals," the heat that dries up the very marrow of the bones. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it of a skin that, become black, "peels off from me," and of bones consumed and set in a glow by a parching heat, taking the whole as the first plain mention of the leprosy that had so disfigured him.

So the witnesses differ a little over the cause of the blackness — whether melancholy, disease, or the scorching sun — but on the picture they are one, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it into a single grim image. Job's skin was black upon him, the blood settled and the sores suppurated and scabbed over; and his bones were burnt with heat, for he lay in a constant fever that "dried up the radical moisture and even consumed the marrow in his bones." From this, Henry bids us "see how frail our bodies are, which carry in themselves the seeds of our own disease and death." Clarke sharpens the second clause into "a strong expression to point out the raging fever that was continually preying upon his vitals," while Gill likens the blackened skin to that of a people wasted by famine, scorched and discoloured till the living man wore the hue of the grave. The witnesses do not divide over the wretchedness the verse fixes: a body blackened without and burning within, the skin peeling from the flesh and the bones parched with fever, so that the man is already, as it were, decaying above ground. The lament has reached the last stage of its descent through the sufferer's frame — from the terror of the soul, through the ache of the bones, to the very skin rotting and the marrow consumed — and there is nothing left of the honoured man of the former chapter but this scorched and blackened ruin, brother indeed to the creatures of the waste.
31:
The long complaint closes on a note of music silenced, and the witnesses let the elegy die away with it — "my harp also is turned to mourning." The reformed John Gill recalls that Job had used the harp as David did, whether in the worship of God or in innocent recreation, and now it is wholly laid aside, so that nothing is heard from him or in his house but the voice of mourning. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse of a harp turned to mourning and a pipe become "the voice of them that weep," and hear in it the deliberate art of the poet: the cheerful music that once belonged to Job's prosperity is turned to gloomy weeping and sobbing, and the whole second part of the monologue is made to die away in these prolonged, vibrating, elegiac strains, Job's last sorrowful lament before the great turn of the book.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it that, instead of the harp, Job's only music now is his own plaintive cries, both the stringed instrument and the pipe fallen mute or used for mournful ditties alone; and he draws from the whole chapter a closing observation, that for all its painful and pathetic sorrow it is tempered with a calmness and humiliation not seen in Job's earlier lamentations — a change he dates from the great confession of ch. 19:25, after which, assured that his Redeemer lives, Job "submitted to his dispensations, kissed the rod, and mourned not without hope." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the close "therefore is my harp turned to mourning, and my pipe into the voice of them that weep," and notes that the two instruments named, like those of Gen. 4:21, are respectively the stringed and the wind. The witnesses do not divide. They hear the chapter end where it must, on the exact reversal of joy: the harp that once sounded festival now sounds grief, the pipe that piped mirth now sobs. Keil hears the poet let the whole second part of the monologue die away in these prolonged, vibrating strains, as one hears the last tremor of a plucked string fade into silence. Yet under the mourning, as Clarke and Keil alike discern, there is no longer the wildness of Job's first outcries but a chastened, hoping sorrow, so that the dying fall of the music is not despair but the last, low grief of a man who has told his misery to the end and waits, though he knows it not, on the very edge of God's answer.
